newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya police battle armed youths near Mombasa.
newsitem.headline: Kenya police battle armed youths near Mombasa.

text.p: Police and the crack General Service Unit (GSU) fought armed youths south of Kenya's Indian Ocean city of Mombasa on Friday two days after six policemen were among 13 people killed by unknown attackers.
"GSU and regular police are battling youths in Ngombeni," a witness told Reuters at Ukunda, on Kenya's lush southcoast, a haven for foreign tourists. Ngombeni is 10 km (six miles) south of Mombasa.
Police reinforcements and the army were being sent to the area, witnesses and security officials told Reuters. The fighting cut the main road to Tanzania and all vehicles were turned back.
"A search operation is on in Ngombeni, we are waiting for information," a police spokesman said.
Fighting began as police hunted dozens of attackers who burned down two police stations at Likoni in Mombasa on Wednesday night, killing 13 people including six policemen.
The well-organised assailants stole police weapons, released prisoners and picked on ordinary civilians, killing several.

Witnesses said people were fleeing the Likoni area on Friday and police and the GSU had found some 15 youths, some with gunshot wounds, while combing adjacent areas. Some of the youths had guns, which were suspected to have been looted from police.
Residents in Mombasa said police, army, navy and general service paramilitary units had launched a huge operation, stretching from the city to the Tanzanian border, to hunt down the killers.
They said the operation, involving hundreds of men, was led by intelligence officers flown in from the capital Nairobi.
Kenyan newspapers reflected confusion among officials and witnesses over the precise identity of the attackers who were described as well-organised "gangsters" on a night-long rampage.

The assailants burned down a tourist police office and a police station, releasing scores of Kenyan prisoners and stealing 30 firearms and thousands of rounds of ammunition in the surprise onslaught, which jolted Kenya's security chiefs.
The attack was launched at a time of high political tension in Kenya ahead of a general election later this year.

In an editorial headlined "What's behind this dastardly attack?'', the independent Daily Nation newspaper ruled out common criminals and said the main objective was probably to seize arms and deliver the message they would kill in cold blood.
It said the Likoni raid was the trickiest security challenge for Kenya since ethnic clashes in the Rift Valley in 1992.
The attack began at about 8.30 p.m. when the tourist police post at Likoni was hit. The post is at the landing point of the ferry from Mombasa Island, separated from Likoni by a narrow sea channel.
Minister of State in the Presidency Jackson Kalweo vowed fast action to track down the dozens of attackers armed with machetes.
Some witnesses said the attackers were local people taking reprisals against Likoni police for alleged brutality. They singled out Kenyan settlers from outside the coastal area before attacking them.
A witness said there appeared to have been at least five groups behind Wednesday's attack. Newspapers said on Friday three policewomen were abducted by the raiders who fled south of Mombasa.
Police sources said they were holding four men suspected of being among the attackers who also wounded at least 30 people.
There were no reports of casualties among the thousands of foreign tourists in the area of Mombasa, which is on the Indian Ocean and is about 500 km (310 miles) southeast of Nairobi.
The last time the area saw serious violence was in December 1992 when the local Digo people attacked settlers from other tribes in a row over a Likoni quarry before a general election.
